video_title: David Rosenberg: “Every Bubble Pops” — Markets Aren’t Ready
gist: Economist David Rosenberg tells Wealthion host Maggie Lake that the AI-era equity market is a bubble located in investor behavior rather than in the technology, citing margin debt up 50% year-over-year to $1.5 trillion against a 25% market gain, a Shiller CAPE of 41, record 78% bullish sentiment, 1% mutual fund cash ratios and a record 73% household equity allocation. He argues the real Q4 surprise will be the labor market rather than inflation or deficits, and describes the low-to-moderate-risk multi-asset Rosie model portfolio (50% equities / 35% bonds / 15% hard assets, heavy in two-year notes, zero technology ETFs) being launched as an ETF with Corton Capital in September.

themes.theme: The bubble is in behavior, not the technology

insights.claim: David Rosenberg is willing to label the current AI-driven equity market a bubble and says it has not popped yet, arguing that every bubble eventually pops and that bubbles typically take one to three years to fester before breaking.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Rosenberg is explicitly not calling a top on timing — he expects the melt-up to persist for a while, so positioning should be about risk management and survivability rather than an immediate short.
insights.quote: this hasn't popped yet but every bubble pops

insights.claim: Rosenberg locates the current bubble in investor behavior and crowd psychology rather than in AI technology itself, which he says is why people resist the bubble label.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If the excess is behavioral rather than technological, sentiment and leverage indicators — not AI revenue forecasts — are the leading signals to monitor for the unwind.
insights.quote: the bubble is not in the technology. The bubble is in investor behavior.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says he was admonished at Merrill Lynch for calling housing a bubble in 2006-2007 and that audiences walked out of his marketing presentations, and he sees the same institutional pushback pattern repeating with AI today.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The intensity of pushback against a bubble call has historically been a signal of how entrenched consensus positioning is — a contrarian confirmation rather than a refutation.
insights.quote: when I was at Maril Lynch and I did marketing and the sales guys that were with me and I went traveling around the states and I had a whole chart book on the housing bubble. People walked out of the room.

insights.claim: Rosenberg frames the AI move as one more iteration of the innovation-curve pattern seen in electricity, the railways, the Nifty Fifty of the late 1960s, the internet and housing finance — all genuine technologies that still produced investor manias.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Accepting that the underlying technology is real does not protect an investor from the valuation and leverage unwind that historically follows innovation booms.

insights.claim: Rosenberg warns that owning the leading names of a technology boom is not protection, citing Nortel and Lucent in 1999 as stocks that performed brilliantly right up until both essentially disappeared.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Concentration in today's AI leaders carries permanent-impairment risk, not just drawdown risk — an argument for diversification away from the index's largest weights.
insights.quote: in 1999, if you own Nortell and you own Lucent, you were doing great up until they both basically disappeared

insights.claim: Margin debt has risen roughly 50% over the past year to about $1.5 trillion while the market itself is up 25%, meaning leverage is expanding at double the rate of prices.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Leverage growing at 2x the index gain is the mechanism that turns a normal correction into a forced-liquidation event; margin debt is the single number to track for the unwind.
insights.quote: margin debt is soared 50% in the past year to $1 half trillion dollars. The market's up 25%, margin debt's up 50, running double.

insights.claim: Rosenberg cites record positioning extremes: bullish sentiment at 78% (never previously that high), portfolio managers and mutual funds down to 1% cash ratios, and the US household sector holding a record 73% of its portfolio in equities versus only 7% in bonds.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: With institutions and households already fully invested, there is no marginal buyer left to absorb selling — the classic setup for an air-pocket decline.
insights.quote: The US household sector, 73% of their portfolio is in equities. It's never been that high before. Only 7% is in bonds.

insights.claim: Rosenberg notes the Shiller CAPE has reached 41 for the first time since 2000, but stresses that valuations are less stretched than the late 1990s and that leverage and sentiment — not the multiple alone — are what make this episode dangerous.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Bears waiting for a 1999-style valuation peak may be watching the wrong gauge; the leverage and cash-ratio data are already at records even though the multiple is not.
insights.quote: the Schiller Cape just went to 41 for the first time since since 2000

insights.claim: Rosenberg argues the price-earnings multiple drives long-run equity performance far more than earnings growth does, describing the multiple as a proxy for confidence.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Forecasting earnings correctly is insufficient — a confidence shock that compresses the multiple can overwhelm strong AI-driven earnings growth.
insights.quote: The multiple is the heartbeat of confidence.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says he treats valuations not as a timing tool but as a directional read on whether the wind is at an investor's back or in their face, and warns that by the time valuations start to matter the damage is already done.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A usable discipline for staying invested in an expensive market while sizing risk down rather than exiting entirely.
insights.quote: people say valuations don't matter till they matter. By the time they matter your head sliced off

themes.theme: Rosie portfolio construction and the ETF launch

insights.claim: Rosenberg is research advisor — not the launching manager — on a global ETF called Rosie being launched with Corton Capital in the second or third week of September, built on the Rosenberg Research model portfolio he started in early 2023.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A new listed vehicle that makes Rosenberg's macro views directly investable, and a disclosure investors should weight when reading his public commentary.

insights.claim: The Rosie model portfolio is up 55% since the start of 2023 with a 0.7 beta to a 60/40 benchmark, a 0.4 beta to the S&P 500 and a Sharpe ratio above one, which Rosenberg offers as evidence a self-described perma-bear can compound capital.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A low-beta multi-asset sleeve that kept pace reasonably well in a melt-up is the kind of hedge that can be held through a top without career risk.

insights.claim: Despite his bearish rhetoric Rosenberg's portfolio currently holds 50% equities, 35% bonds and 15% hard assets such as commodities, with no cash and no short positions, and a large tactical position in two-year Treasury notes as a pure bet on the Fed.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Rosenberg's actual allocation is far less defensive than his commentary implies — the expressed bearishness is in beta and front-end duration, not in cash or shorts.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the portfolio has never owned a single technology stock or technology ETF and has instead played AI indirectly through emerging Asia exposure such as MSCI Asia, picking up Korean and Taiwanese semiconductor content while trimming that risk.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A cheaper, less crowded way to hold AI supply-chain exposure than US mega-cap tech, and a template for de-risking AI beta without abandoning the theme.
insights.quote: we have not owned a tech ETF

insights.claim: Rosenberg targets high-single-digit risk-adjusted returns over a cycle rather than 15%, describing the mandate as designed to bunt for singles — backtested over decades to beat bear markets by at least 10 percentage points while giving up upside in bull markets.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Sets the expectation that this is a portfolio ballast product, not an alpha engine — relevant to sizing it against the 'rocket fuel' portion of a portfolio.
insights.quote: not likely to hit a home run in a bull market, but you won't strike out in a bare market

insights.claim: Rosenberg says he deliberately shuns shorting because negative carry punishes anything short of very high conviction and shorting requires a distinct skill, and he draws on 12 years sitting alongside portfolio managers at Gluskin Sheff running roughly $3 billion in long-short funds.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A bearish macro view expressed through allocation and duration rather than shorts avoids the carry bleed that has destroyed bears in this cycle.

themes.theme: Why long rates are rising — hyperscaler capex, not deficits

insights.claim: Rosenberg rejects the fiscal-deficit explanation for the roughly 60 basis point rise in yields, pointing out that nobody was talking about deficits in February when the 10-year note was at 3.97% and that the twin-deficit story is 40 years old.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If the deficit narrative is not what moved yields, the bond selloff may reverse for reasons the fiscal bears are not watching — supporting a long-duration or front-end trade.
insights.quote: We weren't talking about deficits back in February when the 10-year note was 3.97.

insights.claim: Rosenberg's alternative explanation for higher real rates is that free-cash-flow-negative hyperscalers are funding their AI capex ramp in the capital markets rather than off the balance sheet, and he notes their CDS and credit spreads are already widening.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler credit spreads become the key leading indicator for both the AI capex cycle and the level of real rates — widening spreads would cap the capex bid and relieve rate pressure.
insights.quote: these hyperscalers are like ramping up their capex now. They're not doing it off the balance sheet because they're free cash flow negative.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the US has now run six consecutive years of deficit-to-GDP ratios above 5% with debt-to-GDP over 100%, something never done before even by FDR during the New Deal, and calls it a miracle that the 10-year yield is below 5% with no QE running.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Frames current long-end yields as already resilient in the face of extreme fiscal supply — an argument that the marginal fiscal shock is largely priced.
insights.quote: It's actually a miracle that the 10-year no yields below 5%.

insights.claim: Rosenberg predicts a split government after the November 3 midterms produces two years of fiscal gridlock, and notes that historically when the party in power loses the legislature 80% of the time the economy slows, inflation slows, and the Treasury market stages a large rally.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A datable catalyst for a duration trade: position for a Treasury rally into and after November 3, starting at the front end where Rosenberg says it has already begun.
insights.quote: 80% of the time the economy slows down. 80% of the time inflation slows down. 80% of the time you get a huge rally in the Treasury market.

themes.theme: Fed communication and the equity-market backstop

insights.claim: Rosenberg criticizes the current Fed chair for repeating that inflation is above target without explaining how the Fed will return it to target, calling the communication sloppy and frustrating for the bond market.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Persistent Fed communication ambiguity keeps a risk premium in the curve; any move to clearer guidance would be a catalyst for front-end rates.
insights.quote: Very strange thing uh for the leader of the Fed to be saying uh sloppy,

insights.claim: Rosenberg argues the Fed's dot plots, introduced in 2012 to reassure markets during a disinflationary output gap, have long outlived their usefulness, and that there are far too many Fed speakers — the post-Bernanke Fed vastly over-communicated.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Suggests fading dot-plot-driven rate repricing as noise rather than signal when building front-end positions.
insights.quote: They've way outlived their usefulness.

insights.claim: Rosenberg uses December 2018 as the template for today: Powell hiked and still had two 2019 hikes penciled in, the corporate bond market froze, and the Fed instead cut three times — a year in which being long the front end of the curve paid off.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The explicit historical analogue behind Rosenberg's large two-year note position — the trade works when Fed guidance is violently repriced by credit stress.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the Fed will backstop a destabilizing equity decline but only when it coincides with credit market problems, noting that in 2018 it was credit stress, not falling stocks, that stopped the Fed, and that the 2022 near-30% drawdown was painful but never destabilizing enough to force a pivot.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Credit spreads, not the S&P drawdown, are the trigger to watch for the Fed put — equity investors expecting a rescue on price alone will be early.
insights.quote: you will not have a destabilizing decline in the stock market absent um some sort of problem in the credit market

insights.claim: Rosenberg believes the current Fed chair has a longer fuse and a lower strike price on the Fed put than Powell, Bernanke or Greenspan did, meaning markets would have to fall further before official support arrives.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Investors relying on a 'too big to fail' equity market should assume a deeper drawdown before intervention than in prior cycles.

themes.theme: Labor market as the Q4 surprise

insights.claim: Rosenberg's single biggest call is that the labor market, not inflation, will be the surprise heading into the fourth quarter, precisely because the Fed has stopped paying attention to it.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Positions ahead of a narrative rotation from inflation to employment — bullish front-end Treasuries and bearish cyclicals if payrolls confirm.
insights.quote: I like to focus on things other people aren't focused on

insights.claim: Rosenberg points to a July nonfarm payrolls print of minus 23,000 with a roughly 20,000 monthly average and downward revisions, and expects by the fourth quarter that this negative print will prove to have been no fluke rather than a one-off giveback.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Sequential negative payroll prints in October and November are the specific, datable evidence that would validate the recession trade.
insights.quote: AI or no AI, that'll be difficult to explain that we're not heading into a recession.

insights.claim: Rosenberg argues slowing nominal wage growth reveals more underlying labor slack than the 4.1% unemployment rate implies, because a genuinely tight labor market would not produce visibly decelerating wages.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Wage growth, not the headline U3, is the cleanest real-time read on labor slack — continued deceleration supports the disinflation and rate-cut case.
insights.quote: Nominal wage growth is slowing down visibly. That's telling me that there is more underlying slack being built up than a 4.1% unemployment rate would otherwise suggest.

insights.claim: Rosenberg highlights that the broad U6 measure of underemployment is stuck at 7.9% versus 7.0% just before COVID, and criticizes the Fed for focusing on the lagging U3 headline rate instead.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: U6 running nearly a full point above its pre-COVID level while policy is not easing is the mispricing Rosenberg is trading via the front end.
insights.quote: The broadest measure of unemployment is 7.9. It was 7.0.

insights.claim: Rosenberg reasons that if there is no inflation coming out of the labor market then any cost shock hits a wall there — real wages fall, real consumer spending falls, and demand becomes the referee of inflation after the initial shock.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A transmission model arguing that price shocks are self-limiting without wage validation — the core of Rosenberg's disinflation and bond-bullish case.
insights.quote: demand will be the referee as to what happens with inflation after the initial shock

insights.claim: Rosenberg says he prefers what is unloved and under-owned, singling out bonds and two-year Treasury notes as positions nobody wants to discuss at a cocktail party.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: With households at a record-low 7% bond allocation, the front end offers both contrarian positioning and a direct hedge to the equity leverage he is warning about.
insights.quote: So, I sort of like what's unloved and what's under owned.
